review_target: server/internal/service/access.go and server/internal/service/access_test.go (new domain layer implementing Decisions 3, 5, 10, 11) plus server/internal/service/costing.go (ErrForbidden/ErrConflict addition, house-style reference) — hostile review against user-spec.md, tech-spec.md and tasks/2.md. Note: no `go` toolchain was available in this environment (go build/go test could not be executed), so this review is based on full static reading of both files, not runtime verification.
summary: The domain layer is sound on the two hardest invariants it's responsible for. Decision 10 (admin bypass) is centralized in a single unexported helper, hasEffectiveAccess(user UserRecord) bool { return user.HasAccess || user.Role == RoleAdmin } (access.go:202-204), and both places in this file that need to know 'does this user have access' — GetAccessState (line 127) and CreateRequest (line 146) — call it; there is no code path in this file that reads user.HasAccess raw and treats it as the final answer. Decision 11 (EnsureUser must not reset role/has_access) is enforced structurally, not just by convention: UserRepository.EnsureUser's signature (access.go:64, `EnsureUser(ctx, login, email, displayName string) error`) has no role/has_access parameters at all, so AccessService.EnsureUser (line 103) cannot pass them through even if it wanted to — the type system forecloses the mistake the task exists to prevent. Both are backed by tests that exercise the actual risk (TestAccessService_AdminWithoutAccessFlag_HasAccess, TestAccessService_EnsureUser_DelegatesWithoutResettingRoleAndAccess). Input validation and error handling are minimal but appropriate for a layer with zero direct DB/SQL access and no attacker-facing string ever echoed back: requireLogin only checks emptiness, and every error is wrapped with a fixed, non-parameterized prefix (no login/email/displayName content leaks into error text) — this file introduces no injection or user-enumeration surface itself. The one substantive finding is about the implementer's own flagged trade-off in SetAccess (access.go:168-186): the claim that the accepted GetUser-snapshot race has 'no access impact, has_access stays authoritative' is correct as stated — I traced the write order and the flag write (line 175) always reflects exactly what the admin asked for (`granted`), unaffected by any staleness in the RequestStatus snapshot used afterward — but the claim understates the actual blast radius. The race can silently break the decided_by audit trail that Decision 5 calls 'the only trace of who granted or revoked access,' and in the revoke direction can cause an admin's DecideRequest call to overwrite a request the user *just* submitted (one they never reviewed) rather than the one they intended to act on. See finding 1.

findings.owasp: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (loss of the decided_by attribution trail) / A04:2021 - Insecure Design (accepted race has a wider effect than documented)
findings.location: server/internal/service/access.go:158-198 (SetAccess), specifically the snapshot-vs-decide comment at lines 179-185; also server/internal/service/access.go:138-153 (CreateRequest) which has the symmetric race
findings.description: SetAccess reads the user (and thus RequestStatus) once at the top, writes the has_access flag, and only then decides — based on that stale snapshot, not a fresh read — whether to call DecideRequest at all (lines 186-188: `if user.RequestStatus == "" { return nil }`). The comment at lines 179-185 correctly says the flag write itself is unaffected (verified: it happens at line 175, driven only by the admin-supplied `granted` argument, before the snapshot is even consulted), so the actual authorization outcome an admin requests is never at risk from this race — that part of the implementer's claim holds. What the comment doesn't spell out: (1) Lost audit trail — if a user calls CreateRequest concurrently with an admin's SetAccess(grant=true) for the same login, and CreateRequest's own GetUser read lands before SetAccess's flag write commits, CreateRequest succeeds (hasEffectiveAccess was still false at that read) and creates a fresh pending row. SetAccess's stale snapshot still says RequestStatus=="" from before that race, so it returns early at line 187 and never calls DecideRequest. Net result: the user has access (correct), but the access_requests row is permanently stuck 'pending' with decided_by/decided_at never set — the one place Decision 5's own rationale says the grant is attributed to an admin has no attribution at all for this grant, and the row can never self-correct (any later CreateRequest by that user short-circuits to ErrConflict per line 146-148 since hasEffectiveAccess is now true). (2) Mis-attributed rejection — in the revoke direction, if a user's CreateRequest lands in the narrow window right after SetAccess's flag write (line 175, has_access now false) but before its DecideRequest call, the user's freshly-submitted, never-reviewed request gets silently flipped to 'rejected' with decided_by set to the admin who was revoking a prior grant — not the admin (if any) who will actually look at this new request. An admin later reading access_requests would see a rejection attributed to themselves (or a colleague) for a request neither of them ever saw. Neither scenario lets an attacker gain unintended access — the flag itself is always exactly what the admin asked for — but both scenarios silently corrupt the one accountability mechanism (decided_by) this design explicitly relies on for 'who decided this.'
findings.recommendation: Not necessarily a blocker for this task (the task file explicitly scopes the transactional fix to Task 3/the repository layer, and the code already documents this as an accepted trade-off) — but the documentation should be corrected to say what's actually true: 'has_access is always exactly what the admin requested; the accepted risk is losing or mis-attributing the decided_by/access_requests audit trail for the racing request, not losing or gaining access.' If closing this is ever prioritized, the fix belongs at the repository/transaction layer (Task 3), e.g. have SetAccess's flag update and DecideRequest happen inside one transaction with a fresh read, or have DecideRequest take a WHERE clause that only affects rows still in the state implied by the snapshot (optimistic-concurrency style) so a racing write is detected instead of silently overwritten.

findings.owasp: A04:2021 - Insecure Design (duplication risk for a security-critical rule across layers)
findings.location: server/internal/service/access.go:200-204 (hasEffectiveAccess, unexported); tech-spec.md 'Проверка доступа' section — `RequireAccess` (a later task) is described as reading the user from the DB and applying `has_access || role == 'admin'` itself
findings.description: access.go's own doc comment (lines 85-88) states AccessService is 'the single place where access rules live.' That's true within this file, but hasEffectiveAccess is unexported and only reachable from within the service package. Per the tech-spec's architecture table, AccessService is listed as a consumer used by middleware, but the same tech-spec's 'Проверка доступа' prose describes RequireAccess as itself reading the user record and applying `has_access || role == 'admin'` — which reads as the middleware (a different package, a later task) re-deriving the same boolean rather than necessarily calling through GetAccessState/an exported check. This is not a defect in the code reviewed here — Task 2 is explicitly service-layer-only and no handler/middleware files exist yet in server/internal/handler/ (confirmed: only auth.go, cors.go, http.go, metrics.go present, no middleware.go or access.go handler). It's a forward-looking risk: if the later task reimplements the boolean instead of consuming AccessService's own computed AccessState.HasAccess, the 'one place' invariant this task establishes stops being true in practice, and a future edit to hasEffectiveAccess (e.g. adding a third bypass condition) could silently fail to propagate to the enforcement point that actually gates requests.
findings.recommendation: Flag for whoever implements the middleware task: prefer calling AccessService.GetAccessState(ctx, login) and reading .HasAccess (which already applies Decision 10 correctly) over re-reading UserRecord and re-deriving the OR condition in the handler package. If a narrower, allocation-light method is wanted for the hot middleware path, consider exporting a small `HasAccess(ctx, login) (bool, error)` wrapper around the same private helper rather than duplicating the boolean expression.

findings.owasp: A01:2021 - Broken Access Control (defense-in-depth / trust boundary documentation)
findings.description: SetAccess performs the actual privilege-changing operation (toggling has_access for an arbitrary login) with zero internal authorization check — it trusts the caller completely. This is the correct layering per the tech-spec (RequireAdmin gates this at the handler/middleware level, a later task), and the doc comment does call it 'админская операция.' But there's no explicit statement of the precondition the method relies on (caller must have already verified the acting principal is role=='admin'), unlike, say, decidedBy's emptiness check which does document why it's required. Since this is the one method in the whole feature capable of granting or revoking access for any user, a one-line precondition comment would make the trust boundary explicit for anyone wiring a new caller to this method in the future (e.g. a self-service endpoint added later that forgets to route through RequireAdmin).
findings.recommendation: Add a comment to SetAccess's doc block stating explicitly that the method performs no authorization check itself and requires the caller (handler/middleware) to have already verified the acting principal is an admin — e.g. 'SetAccess assumes the caller has already verified admin privileges for the acting principal; it performs no authorization check of its own.'

findings.description: requireLogin only checks for empty/whitespace-only input (`strings.TrimSpace(login) == ""`); there's no upper bound on length or restriction on control characters before the value is handed to the repository (Task 3) and ultimately a `VARCHAR(255)` column. For the primary path (login sourced from the authenticated OAuth session per Decision 1) this is low risk since the value isn't attacker-supplied at this layer. For SetAccess specifically, `login` is the `{login}` URL path segment supplied directly by an authenticated admin — an already-trusted principal per the threat model, so impact is limited, but an oversized or control-character-laden value would currently sail through this layer and only be caught (or not) by whatever the repository/DB does with it in Task 3.
findings.recommendation: Optional hardening, not a blocker: bound login length in requireLogin (e.g. reject > 255 chars to match the schema) so the service layer fails fast with ErrInvalidArgument instead of relying on the repository/DB to reject or silently truncate an oversized value. Low priority given the caller is always an authenticated principal at this layer today.

findings.owasp: A01:2021 - Broken Access Control (verification only — no user enumeration found)
findings.location: server/internal/service/access.go — GetAccessState (114-130) and SetAccess (158-198), both propagate ErrNotFound via GetUser
findings.description: Checked whether ErrNotFound propagation creates a login-enumeration or timing oracle. It doesn't, for both call sites: GetAccessState's `login` comes from the caller's own authenticated session (per Decision 1/tech-spec, not from arbitrary request input), so an ErrNotFound here can only ever be about the caller's own identity, not a probe of other accounts. SetAccess's `login` is the admin-only `{login}` path parameter; the caller (an admin) already has full visibility into which logins exist via ListUsers, so a 404 for an unknown login discloses nothing an admin doesn't already have. No timing-based enumeration risk was found at this layer either — there's no differential branching in access.go based on whether an account exists versus is merely access-restricted; both paths call the same GetUser and return the same wrapped error shape.
findings.recommendation: None — recorded as verified, not a new finding.

findings.owasp: A03:2021 - Injection (verification only — no SQL/injection surface in this file)
findings.description: This file contains zero direct database or SQL access — it's entirely interface-based (UserRepository, AccessRequestRepository), consistent with the task's stated scope and the house style referenced from costing.go. All error messages built with fmt.Errorf use fixed, non-parameterized prefixes ('get user:', 'create access request:', 'set access:', 'decide access request:', etw.) and never interpolate login/email/displayName/decidedBy into the error text, so there's no path for those values to leak via error messages at this layer even before Decision 17's fixed-text handler mapping (a later task) is applied. Whitespace-only login/decidedBy values are rejected via strings.TrimSpace before reaching any repository call, and no string concatenation of user input into any command/query exists to sanitize in the first place.
findings.recommendation: None — recorded as verified, not a new finding.
